title: Weather and seasons
goal: Talk about the weather, the seasons and temperature — and learn to compare two things, which in Hebrew takes just two small words.
bekal: comparing two things with יוֹתֵר and פָּחוֹת

dialogs.title: שִׂיחָה — חַם מִדַּי
dialogs.intro: Budi and Yossi are sitting on the balcony in August.

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.id: It's so hot! How many degrees is it today?

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.id: It's hot in Indonesia, but not like this.

lines.speaker: יוֹסִי:
lines.text: בְּתֵל אָבִיב הַקַּיִץ יוֹתֵר לַח מִירוּשָׁלַיִם.
lines.baca: betel aviv hakayits yoter lakh miyerushalayim.
lines.id: In Tel Aviv the summer is more humid than in Jerusalem.
lines.literal: in-tel aviv the-summer more humid from-jerusalem.

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.id: And in winter? Does it snow?

lines.speaker: יוֹסִי:
lines.text: בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם לִפְעָמִים. פֹּה כִּמְעַט אַף פַּעַם לֹא.
lines.baca: biyerushalayim lif'amim. poh kim'at af pa'am lo.
lines.id: In Jerusalem sometimes. Here almost never.
lines.literal: in-jerusalem sometimes. here almost even-once not.

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.id: So what is there in winter?

lines.speaker: יוֹסִי:
lines.id: Rain, lots of rain. And strong wind.

lines.speaker: בּוּדִי:
lines.id: When's the nicest time in Israel?

lines.speaker: יוֹסִי:
lines.text: אָבִיב. אַפְּרִיל וּמַאי — לֹא חַם וְלֹא קַר.
lines.baca: aviv. april umai — lo kham velo kar.
lines.id: Spring. April and May — not hot, not cold.
lines.literal: spring. april and-may — not hot and-not cold.

lines.speaker: יוֹסִי:
lines.text: אוֹתוֹ דָּבָר. תָּמִיד אוֹתוֹ דָּבָר בָּאוֹגוּסְט.
lines.baca: oto davar. tamid oto davar ba'ogust.
lines.id: The same. It's always the same in August.
lines.literal: that-same thing. always that-same thing in-august.

notes: **אֵיזֶה חֹם!** literally "which heat!" but it means "it's so hot!". אֵיזֶה + noun is how Israelis exclaim: אֵיזֶה יֹפִי! (how lovely!), אֵיזֶה בַּלָּגָן! (what a mess!). Used constantly, and it instantly makes your Hebrew sound alive.

⚠️ **חַם and חֹם are different.** חַם (*kham*) is the adjective "hot": הַיּוֹם חַם. חֹם (*khom*) is the noun "heat/temperature": אֵיזֶה חֹם! Just one vowel apart — and without niqqud both are spelled חם.
**Weather is stated without a subject**: הַיּוֹם חַם ("today hot"), קַר בַּחוּץ ("cold outside"). Hebrew has no word like the *it* in *it is hot*.

**יוֹתֵר ... מִ־** = "more ... than". The order: יוֹתֵר + adjective + מִ + what you compare with. For the opposite use **פָּחוֹת** (less). For "the most" use **הֲכִי**: הֲכִי נָעִים (the most pleasant).
⚠️ **מִ־ attaches to the thing you compare with**: יוֹתֵר לַח **מִ**ירוּשָׁלַיִם. Not a separate word. It's the same prefix as "from" in unit 2 — Hebrew uses one word for both "from" and "than".
**רוּחַ (wind) is feminine** even without the ־ָה ending — one of the five exceptions mentioned in unit 3. Hence רוּחַ חֲזָקָה, not חָזָק.
**יוֹרֵד** ("comes down") is used for rain and snow: יוֹרֵד גֶּשֶׁם (it's raining), יוֹרֵד שֶׁלֶג. Hebrew has no separate verb "to rain" — it uses "come down", like English "the rain is coming down".
**אוֹתוֹ דָּבָר** ("the same thing") — a very common set phrase. Note that אוֹתוֹ here is not the object "him" from unit 7 but "that same". The sentence tells you which.

grammars.title: Comparing: three words and you're done
body: Hebrew doesn't change the adjective to compare — there's no *big → bigger → biggest*. It just adds a word in front, like English *more* and *most*.
after: ⚠️ **מִדַּי = "too"**, and it comes **after** the adjective: חַם מִדַּי, יָקָר מִדַּי, מְאֻחָר מִדַּי. The reverse of English, which puts "too" in front.
Some adjectives have a shorter comparative of their own that's used more often: טוֹב → יוֹתֵר טוֹב or **עָדִיף** (better/preferable).

grammars.title: Seasons, months and weather
body: Israel has four seasons on paper, but only two you really feel: a long, dry summer and a short rainy season.
after: ⚠️ The word **אָבִיב** (spring) is part of the name **תֵּל אָבִיב** — "hill of spring". Now the city's name means something to you, not just a sound.

The Western month names are used as they are, in Hebrew sounds: יָנוּאָר, פֶבְּרוּאָר, מֶרְץ, אַפְּרִיל, מַאי, יוּנִי, יוּלִי, אוֹגוּסְט, סֶפְּטֶמְבֶּר, אוֹקְטוֹבֶּר, נוֹבֶמְבֶּר, דֶּצֶמְבֶּר. Israel also has its own Hebrew calendar for holidays, with months like תִּשְׁרֵי and נִיסָן — but for everyday life, the Gregorian calendar is what's used.

blocks.title: Ready-made weather sentences
items: **מָה מֶזֶג הָאֲוִיר הַיּוֹם?** — what's the weather like today?
**הַיּוֹם חַם / קַר / נָעִים** — today it's hot / cold / pleasant.
**חַם מִדַּי בִּשְׁבִילִי** — it's too hot for me.
**מָחָר יִהְיֶה יוֹתֵר קַר** — tomorrow will be colder.

blocks.text: In Israel, as everywhere, the weather is the safest way to start talking to a stranger. These three sentences work almost anywhere, and you already know all their parts:

items: **אֵיזֶה חֹם הַיּוֹם, נָכוֹן?** — hot today, isn't it? The word **נָכוֹן?** ("right?") at the end is how Israelis ask for agreement, like "isn't it?".
**סוֹף סוֹף יוֹרֵד גֶּשֶׁם!** — finally it's raining! In a country short of water, rain is good news, and saying this makes you sound like a local right away.
**מָחָר יִהְיֶה יוֹתֵר נָעִים** — tomorrow will be nicer. A hopeful line that wraps up any weather chat.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Rain in Israel is precious in a way that's hard to imagine from a rainy country.** The dry season lasts six full months without a single drop, so the first rain in October — called **יוֹרֶה** *(yoreh)* — is truly celebrated. Complain about rain in Israel and you'll get the look you'd get complaining about sunshine in London.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with יוֹתֵר, פָּחוֹת or הֲכִי.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: הַיּוֹם חַם מְאוֹד. — יוֹרֵד גֶּשֶׁם בַּחוּץ. — מָחָר יִהְיֶה יוֹתֵר קַר. — יָקָר מִדַּי בִּשְׁבִילִי. — בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם לִפְעָמִים יוֹרֵד שֶׁלֶג.
הַיּוֹם חַם מִדַּי — יוֹרֵד גֶּשֶׁם בַּחוּץ — הַחֹרֶף יוֹתֵר קַר מֵהַקַּיִץ — כַּמָּה מַעֲלוֹת הַיּוֹם
wave: Every morning for a week, write one weather sentence in Hebrew before you leave the house. Seven sentences, seven days — and weather stops being something you have to think about.
